Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Working diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by viral illness or allergen exposure.  
- Key supporting findings from transcript: History of childhood asthma with prior inhaler use; current wheeze and dyspnea; increased use of reliever inhaler in the past; fever noted; patient unable to complete sentences at times during exertion; plan to increase inhaled therapy and arrange follow-up.  
- Considerations (from DDx, consistent with transcript):  
  - Viral upper respiratory infection triggering bronchospasm.  
  - Allergic asthma/allergic rhinitis interplay (hay fever history).  
  - Acute bronchitis as a possible concurrent airway inflammation.  
- Summary of differential diagnoses (from DDx):  
  - Acute asthma exacerbation — High likelihood. Consistent with history of childhood asthma, current wheeze, dyspnea, past albuterol use; triggers include infection/allergens; plan to escalate inhaled therapy.  
  - Viral upper respiratory infection triggering bronchospasm — Medium likelihood. Fever and cough noted; could precipitate asthma flare.  
  - Allergic asthma/allergic rhinitis interplay — Medium likelihood. History of hay fever supports atopy contributing to airway hyperreactivity.  
- Plan actions:  
  - Increase inhaled reliever therapy to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours as needed; provide spacer and educate on use (pharmacist to demonstrate). If high temperature or worsening wheeze, repeat contact means to seek urgent advice.  
  - Prescribe/offer peak flow meter to monitor airway function and record readings; arrange review once readings are available or within about 1 week.  
  - Consider initiation of additional controller therapy after review if symptoms persist or recur.  
  - Recommend regular antihistamine for allergic rhinitis; provide notes with recommended agent (pharmacy can supply).  
  - Arrange a follow-up contact in about a week to assess response and adjust therapy as needed.  
  - If symptoms worsen or patient cannot speak in full sentences, seek urgent care.

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification: Inhaler technique with spacer; use of peak flow monitoring; potential initiation of controller therapy; antihistamine use for allergic rhinitis; return precautions if fever worsens or breathing deteriorates.  
- Patient health goals and priorities: Symptom relief, improved breathing with regular inhaled therapy, guidance on trigger avoidance, and follow-up to optimize management.

- Referrals (allied health, Quitline, AOD services, Aboriginal health worker, or social supports): Not recorded.  
- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled: Follow-up planned in about 1 week; earlier contact if worsening symptoms.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Acute asthma exacerbation — High: Consistent with childhood asthma history, current wheeze and dyspnea, prior reliever use, and clinician’s framing of an asthma flare; triggers potential viral infection or allergen exposure.  
- Viral upper respiratory infection triggering bronchospasm — Medium: Fever and cough with recent onset; may precipitate or contribute to asthma symptoms.  
- Allergic asthma/allergic rhinitis interplay — Medium: History of hay fever supports atopy and allergic-related airway hyperreactivity contributing to symptoms.

● Missing but clinically expected elements: Vital signs (BP, pulse, O2 sat) and objective auscultation findings not documented. Immunisation status not recorded. Lifestyle details partially captured; full smoking/alcohol history limited to stated items.  
● Internal conflicts or contradictions between transcript and DDx: None identified; DDx aligns with transcript (asthma history, wheeze, shortness of breath, possible viral trigger).  
● Transcript quality notes: Clear patient-reported symptoms; some details about prior asthma management are uncertain (past inhaler types and exact dosing not documented).
